name: Gareth Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. This is confidential. What is an ordinary shift like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 58 and a junior operator on the carton-forming press at a packaging plant. I left after secondary school and only moved onto this machine last year. I line up the blanks, watch for glue spots and stop the feed when a carton folds crooked. The senior operator still checks my changeovers.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How are things at home, and do you use AI?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife works part-time at a childcare centre and our grown children have their own places. Our flat rent takes a lot of my below-average operator wage. We have less than a month's expenses put by, and there are few other carton plants close enough for a daily trip. I use AI now and then for a recipe or a plain-language explanation, once I can check the answer. I'd like to stop at 67 if our actual income can cover the bills; I have no number that proves it yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the packing crew that the clever software did not straighten a crooked carton. A person still has to stop the feed, clear the glued flap and get the machine running safely. I do not want a sales pitch used to hold our wages down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am pleased to keep learning this press, but a quiet technology story does not fix our tight rent budget. The childcare centre gives my wife part-time hours, not a second full wage. I'd want a proper count before promising myself retirement at 67.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep doing the handover check with the senior operator and record the stoppages I cause or clear. I'll put a little from each full-pay week into the household reserve after rent. At our shop-floor meeting, I'll ask the delegate to put junior operator rates and notice of roster cuts on the agenda.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, because even today's wages barely leave a margin. A quiet AI forecast leaves the rent due on the same day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes a carton fail after it leaves you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The carton comes out square until the glued seam pulls open on the next belt. I stop the feed and show the faulty blank to the senior operator before we waste another stack. That is a better use of my hands than pretending the press is cleverer than it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How regular are the childcare hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My wife gets extra childcare shifts in some weeks, then none in others. We pay rent from the hours actually worked, not from a hoped-for full rota. I will not call 67 a retirement date until we have checked the income against those costs.

say: **Carton seams** still need a person to stop the press and check the next belt.
A quiet AI story should not excuse **low junior pay** at this plant.
think: The **flat rent** already consumes most of a junior operator wage.
Part-time childcare hours make a **retirement target** at 67 uncertain until income is counted.
do: **Keep** checking the press with the senior operator and record stoppages.
**Save** new money from full-pay weeks after rent and ask the delegate about junior rates.
feel: **Anxious** about current bills even if AI changes little.
S0.quote: A quiet AI forecast leaves the rent due on the same day.
fieldNote: Gareth is a **58-year-old junior** with secondary schooling, lower operator pay and less than a month saved.
His **new savings** depend on full paid weeks; the delegate request concerns existing rates and notice, not a promised raise.

steps.text: Keep recording carton stoppages with senior operator
Save new money from full-pay weeks after rent
Ask shop delegate to raise junior rates and roster notice

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say planning software could change orders long before robots handle cartons. I can use a checked screen when it gives a useful answer, but I still need a person to show me a safe press changeover. People on the junior rate should get paid time to learn it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A new screen could take some checking work from our shift. The concern is whether the plant cuts paid hours while I still have rent and my wife has only part-time wages. I could learn a better changeover method if the place and paid time are real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask the supervisor for the actual roster and any training offer in writing, then bring the pay and hours to our shop delegate. If a paid guarded course place is offered, I'll enrol and practise the changeover with the senior operator. I will keep using AI only for small explanations that I can verify, not to set the press blindly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about hours, though I would rather have a few years' warning than find an empty rota. A promise of training does not pay Friday's rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a safe changeover course include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to stop the press, set the guides, test a short run and show that the glue seam holds. The senior operator should sign off while I practise behind the guard. Reading an AI explanation at home would not qualify me to do that alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which paid hours would you compare?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the new roster with my last four payslips, especially paid changeover time. If shifts are reduced, the delegate needs the actual number before we ask for notice or extra hours. A forecast from a manager is not a paid week.

say: **Order planning** may change before physical carton work does.
Junior operators need **paid guarded practice** when the plant changes the press routine.
think: A cut to **paid hours** would hurt a household already short of reserve.
Occasional checked AI explanations are useful, but **hands-on qualification** needs supervised press time.
do: **Check** written roster and pay before the delegate raises a lost-hour claim.
**Enrol** if a paid guarded changeover place is offered, then practise with the senior operator.
feel: **Anxious** about real paid-hour cuts despite time to adjust.
S1.quote: A promise of training does not pay Friday's rent.
fieldNote: His **occasional AI use** remains limited to checked explanations; it is not a claim of new machine qualification.
A **course enrolment** depends on an offered paid guarded place, while any hours complaint uses the written roster and payslips.

steps.text: Compare written roster with four recent payslips
Bring documented paid-hour cuts to shop delegate
Enrol in changeover course if paid guarded place offered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that if thinking AI can run orders by 2028 and capable robots handle cartons around 2031, our press line could be thinned before I am 63. That is too early to count on stopping work. I want the plant to say which shifts it expects to keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect a large loss of paid shifts when the robots can feed and fold cartons. Our reserve is under a month and I cannot turn 63 into a safe retirement date. I have already lain awake when the plant cancelled a short run; this would be worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll bring the short-run cancellations and pay slips to the shop delegate and push for written notice and paid retraining. If they offer a funded paid place with guarded practice, I'll learn packaging quality checks. If my press hours disappear, I will apply to posted local warehouse or packing roles only if the safe hours and net wage after travel cover rent. A quality post would also need my completed qualification.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I can picture the roster dropping to two days while the rent stays full. I have already lost sleep over one cancelled run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would packaging quality training teach?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The quality course should teach me to spot weak seams, measure a carton and stop a faulty batch. I need supervised practice on the actual guarded line, with fees covered and the hours paid. I cannot finance tuition from the rent reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes an outside job workable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check the posted base wage, shift time and bus fare. If a warehouse job leaves us less after travel than the rent needs, it is not a rescue. I would only apply to a quality opening after I pass the practical test.

say: **2031 robots** could remove press shifts while I am only 63.
The plant owes junior operators **written notice** of actual roster changes.
think: A major **shift loss** would leave less than one month of reserve.
Age **63** is not an affordable retirement date without documented household income.
do: **Push** with the delegate for notice and a funded paid practical place.
**Train** if offered, then apply for real safe local work only when net pay and qualification fit.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected major lost hours and remembered sleeplessness.
S2.quote: I can picture the roster dropping to two days while the rent stays full.
fieldNote: He **expects major lost hours** around age 63 and cites prior lost sleep; the alarmed mood follows that income risk.
Both **outside applications** need real local safe postings and adequate net pay; the quality role additionally needs completed practical qualification.

steps.text: Ask delegate for written notice and funded paid guarded training
Enrol in packaging quality if funded paid guarded place offered
Apply to posted safe local warehouse if displaced and net pay covers rent
Apply to posted safe local quality if qualified, displaced, net pay covers rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI may settle the order sheet in 2031, with robots at the press about 2034. That puts me at 63 and 66. Five years' notice is useful only if we get real paid practice and do not spend it all waiting for a meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 66 I may still need the press wage. My wife's childcare hours come and go, and a small savings pot cannot fund years of rent. If we have enough documented income to stop at 67, fine; I will not plan it as guaranteed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll add money from each full-pay week to our reserve after rent, and ask the delegate to secure a funded paid place in carton quality. If a guarded trainer place is actually offered, I'll attend and take the practical check. After qualifying, if press shifts fall, I'll apply to posted local quality roles only if their safe hours and net wage after bus fare keep the household afloat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, because I can see an hour cut before I can afford to stop. Extra warning gives me a chance to count and train, not a new income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What must the practical check show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The test needs to catch a split seam in a real stack, not just an answer on a screen. I would want the trainer to watch me stop the guarded line and reject a faulty batch. My ordinary AI questions do not teach those hands-on steps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a local quality posting need to say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I need the base wage, the paid shift length and the bus fare from an actual local posting. If those leave less for rent than the press does, I will not take it. Reaching 67 will not cover the bus fare or the flat.

say: **2031 AI** may change orders before robots reach the press around 2034.
Five years matters if operators receive **paid practice** in time.
think: At **66**, household wages may still be needed for rent.
A hoped-for stop at **67** needs real income figures, not an assumed payment.
do: **Save** new money from full-pay weeks after rent.
**Attend** funded paid guarded quality training if offered, then seek a viable posted local role if qualified and hours fall.
feel: **Anxious** about an hour cut before retirement is affordable.
S3.quote: Reaching 67 will not cover the bus fare or the flat.
fieldNote: The **new deposits** use current wages after rent; no existing savings are recounted as a new action.
A **quality application** needs paid guarded training, qualification, lost hours and a posted safe local role at viable net pay.

steps.text: Save new money from full-pay weeks after rent
Ask delegate for funded paid guarded quality place
Attend quality training if funded paid guarded place offered
Apply for posted safe local quality if qualified, hours fall, net pay sufficient

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that AI handling order planning by 2036 would come when I am 68, and able robots at the press around 2039 when I am 71. The decade helps me count the money. It does not promise that I can stop at 67.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would like to be retired before a robot handles the cartons, but the flat and food have to be covered from real income. We have very little saved. If 67 is not affordable, I may still be working when the new systems arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep the press job while it pays and put a little from full weeks into our reserve. This year my wife and I will list rent, food and documented income and ask for retirement figures we can check. If those numbers make stopping at 67 affordable, I'll stop then. If I am still working after 2036 and hours fall, I'll apply to posted safe local packing jobs only when net pay after travel covers our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about whether I can afford to stop, even with ten years of warning. I can choose a date on paper; I cannot choose the amount in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which figures would support stopping?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We need the actual monthly income available after work ends, not a guess that some benefit will arrive. Then we can set it beside rent, food and transport. Until that matches, the press wage remains part of the plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you seek a later packing job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The posting must show a safe shift I can do and a base wage that survives the bus fare. I would only send an application if I were still working and our hours had gone down. An empty promise of local openings is no use.

say: **2036 AI** and later robots leave time to count work and household income.
An age **67 retirement** remains a wish until bills can actually be paid.
think: The **thin reserve** cannot bridge years without a press wage.
If retirement is unaffordable, I may be **working after 2036** when shifts change.
do: **Save** new wages after rent and check documented income against household costs.
**Apply** only if still working after 2036, hours fall and a real safe local job pays enough net.
feel: **Anxious** about retirement affordability despite a long lead time.
S4.quote: I can choose a date on paper; I cannot choose the amount in the bank.
fieldNote: The **retirement enquiry** establishes figures and does not imply entitlement, an early exit or a guaranteed stop at 67.
Any **post-2036 application** requires him still to be employed, fewer paid hours and a posted safe local role with bill-covering net pay.

steps.text: Save new money from full-pay press weeks after rent
Compare documented retirement income with rent and food
Apply to posted safe local packing if still employed after 2036, hours fall, net pay sufficient

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which worries you most, and what would help?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast 2028 case worries me most. I could lose much of the press rota around 63, years before we know whether stopping is affordable. Written hours, a funded paid safe quality place and real local postings with enough money after travel would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what happens to the first carton after it leaves my press. A square carton can still split at the glued seam.

headlineQuote: A square carton can still split at the glued seam.
portrait: **Gareth**, 58, is a junior carton-press operator with secondary schooling and occasional checked AI use.
He and his part-time childcare-worker wife have **grown children**, low pay, flat rent, under a month saved and few local carton plants.
His **progressive outlook** takes hours and training requests to the shop delegate; he will use proven screens alongside supervised press practice.
He is **alarmed** by a fast expected rota loss; a stop at 67 depends on documented household income covering costs.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could bring press robots around 2031 and cut paid shifts before retirement is affordable.
whatWouldHelp: **Written hours**, funded paid guarded quality training and posted safe local work with adequate net pay would help.
